title: Shop math and materials
summary: Area and volume formulas, the Pythagorean theorem and the 3-4-5 squaring trick, and ways to find a height from a shadow or an angle. It also gives slope and grade, the densities of common materials, and what a cubic metre or a 55-gallon drum of water weighs.

steps.text: Pick the section for your job: area and volume, squaring, height, slope, or weight.
Put every length in one unit before using a formula, and convert with the NIST factors if you must mix metric and imperial.
steps.warn: A US gallon (3.785 L) is not an imperial gallon (4.546 L).

steps.text: For weight, work out the volume, multiply by the density from the table, then add the container or frame.
Plan lifting and rigging with the safety factors at the end, and check the real rating on the equipment.
steps.warn: Density figures are typical values. Alloys, moisture and fill level change real weights.

notes:
## Area and volume
Use r for radius (half the diameter). Keep every length in the same unit.

| Shape | Formula |
|---|---|
| Rectangle area | length × width (MathWorld) |
| Circle | circumference 2πr, area πr² (MathWorld) |
| Box (prism) volume | base area × height (U Houston) |
| Cylinder volume | πr²h (U Houston) |
| Cone volume | (1/3)πr²h (U Houston) |
| Sphere volume | (4/3)πr³ (MathWorld) |

π is about 3.14. Example: a round tank 1 m across and 1.5 m tall holds π × 0.5² × 1.5 = 1.18 m³, which is 1,178 L (1 m³ = 1,000 L). Conversions: 1 US gallon = 3.785 L, 1 imperial (Canadian) gallon = 4.546 L, 1 lb = 0.4536 kg, 1 ft = 0.3048 m, 1 ft² = 0.0929 m², 1 ft³ = 0.02832 m³, 1 lb/ft³ = 16.02 kg/m³ (NIST).

## Pythagoras and squaring
- In a right triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the longest side, opposite the right angle (MathWorld).
- **3-4-5 trick:** from a corner, measure 3 along one line. Measure 4 along a line at roughly a right angle. Adjust until the gap between the two marks is exactly 5. Use multiples (6-8-10, 9-12-15) for bigger layouts (US Army).
- A rectangle is square when both diagonals are equal. A diagonal is √(length² + width²) (US Army, MathWorld).

## Height from a shadow or an angle
- **Shadow:** tree height / tree shadow = your height / your shadow. Measure at the same time of day, in sun, on flat ground (Franklin Institute). So tree height = tree shadow x (stick height / stick shadow).
- **Angle (clinometer):** stand D away on level ground. Measure the angle up to the top (A1) and to the base (A2, negative if below eye level). Height = D × (tan A1 − tan A2) (American Forests).
- Example: D = 30 m, A1 = 40°, A2 = −3° gives 30 × (0.839 + 0.052) = 26.7 m.
- The method assumes the top is directly above the base, so a leaning tree or pole gives errors (American Forests).

## Slope and grade
Percent slope = rise ÷ run × 100. Angle = arctan(rise ÷ run) (USGS, Esri).

| Slope | Percent | Angle |
|---|---|---|
| 1 in 12 | 8.33 % | 4.8° |
| 1 in 2 | 50 % | 26.5° (USGS) |
| 1 in 1 | 100 % | 45° (Esri) |

A 1:12 slope is the steepest running slope allowed for a US (ADA) ramp, with at most 760 mm (30 in) of rise per run (Access Board). Run needed = rise ÷ slope, so a ramp that climbs 0.5 m at 1:12 needs 6 m of run.

## Density and weight
Weight = volume × density.

| Material | kg/m³ | lb/ft³ |
|---|---|---|
| Water | 1,000 (USGS) | 62.4 |
| Steel | 7,850 (Iowa DOT, USDA FPL) | 490 |
| Aluminium | 2,700 (NIST) | 169 |
| Copper | 8,960 (NIST) | 559 |
| Lead | 11,350 (NIST) | 709 |
| Concrete, normal | 2,240 to 2,400 (Iowa DOT) | 140 to 150 |
| Gasoline | 720 to 760 (NIOSH) | 45 to 47 |
| Diesel | about 840 (OSHA) | about 52.5 |
| Wood, oven-dry | 320 to 720 for most species (USDA FPL) | 20 to 45 |

Wood weighs more when damp: at 100 % moisture content it holds as much water as wood (USDA FPL). White ash at 12 % moisture is 678 kg/m³ (42.2 lb/ft³) (USDA FPL). Example: a steel plate 2 m × 1 m × 10 mm is 0.02 m³, so about 157 kg.

Gasoline and diesel float on water (specific gravity under 1). Per US gallon, gasoline is about 2.7 to 2.9 kg (6.0 to 6.3 lb) and diesel about 3.2 kg (7.0 lb), calculated from the figures above. A 10 mm steel round bar weighs about 0.62 kg per metre (π × 0.005² × 7,850).

## Water weights
- 1 L of water is 1 kg. 1 m³ is 1,000 kg. 1 US gallon is 8.33 lb (USGS).
- A 55-gallon drum holds 208 L (Greif), so 208 kg or about 458 lb of water. A closed steel drum weighs about 17 kg (38 lb) empty, so a full one is about 225 kg (497 lb) (Repackify).
- "55 gallons" means US gallons. An imperial gallon is 4.546 L (NIST).

## Safety factors that are sourced
Rope 5:1, or 10:1 for life support (Samson). Cribbing at least 4:1 (Virginia DMME). Web straps 3:1 (RAC). No simple safe rule for beams is given here, because span depends on species, grade and size. Use published span tables or an engineer.
